title: Changing Someone's Mind
blurb: Give opinions and try to change someone's opinion

steps.html:
Two people list the qualities a good teacher needs, disagree about nearly all of them, and end up with a list neither of them started with. That is what changing somebody's mind actually looks like.

  • Follow a disagreement and track where each speaker moves
  • Concede a point and then push back
  • Watch a documentary about a period of invention
  • Write a summary of an argument

steps.title: Before you listen: can a teacher be too kind?
steps.sub: Choose the closest to your view.

options.label: No — kindness is never the problem
It depends entirely on the student
I have never thought about it

steps.title: Listen to the first part. What does M think matters most?
options: Being creative and having good ideas.
steps.why: 'For me, the most important quality of a teacher is being patient… and being kind is important, too.'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: J thinks kindness and patience are enough on their own.
steps.why: 'If they're actually going to teach you something, they need to be more than kind and patient.'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: M accepts that a fun lesson is not automatically a useful one.
steps.why: 'Sometimes teachers create really fun lessons, but you don't really learn anything.'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: M says she is against having fun in class.
steps.why: 'I'm all for having fun, but I do want to get more than that out of the class.'

steps.title: Listen to the second part and answer.
steps.prompt: What does J say personally?
options: That a good teacher is quite strict.
That a good teacher should never be strict.
That strictness does not matter either way.
steps.answer: That a good teacher is quite strict.
steps.why: 'Personally, I think a good teacher is quite strict.'

steps.title: Listen to the second part and answer.
steps.prompt: How does M reply?
options: She agrees at once and says she had the same kind of teacher.
She asks whether that kind of teacher is a bit old-fashioned.
She changes the subject to something that happened to her instead.
steps.answer: She asks whether that kind of teacher is a bit old-fashioned.
steps.why: 'Isn't that kind of teacher a bit old-fashioned?' — a challenge in the form of a question.

steps.title: Listen to the second part and answer.
steps.prompt: What is the list they end up with?
options: Motivating, supportive, creative, hard-working, well organised.
They never agree on a list.
steps.answer: Motivating, supportive, creative, hard-working, well organised.
steps.why: Neither of them started with that list, which is the point of the recording.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.prompt: Neither speaker's original list survives. What does that show about the conversation?
options: Both of them gave up on their own view.
Each conceded something and took something from the other, and the list improved.
steps.answer: Each conceded something and took something from the other, and the list improved.
steps.why: M concedes creativity, J concedes motivating and supportive, and both add hard-working and organised. That is what a productive disagreement does.

options: You need enough money, and you can do what you enjoy in your free time.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: M does not disagree directly. She asks whether that kind of teacher is a bit old-fashioned.
steps.prompt: What is she doing?
options: Asking a genuine question about teaching history.
Disagreeing, but framing it as a question so that the other speaker can retreat without losing face.
Changing the subject because she has no view.
steps.answer: Disagreeing, but framing it as a question so that the other speaker can retreat without losing face.
steps.why: A question with a bit in it is a hedge. She has stated a position and left the other speaker room to adjust.

steps.title: Why arguments are so often written in the passive
steps.html:
Recycled: the passive and the causative do most of the quiet work in a persuasive text.

A persuasive text presents a claim as a settled fact by removing the person who made it. It is widely believed that… It has been argued that… Nothing is gained by… The passive lets you avoid saying who thinks so.

That is a legitimate tool and also a warning. When you read it is thought that, ask by whom? — and when you write it, be sure you could answer.

The causative appears in the practical half of an argument, because proposals are about arranging things: Staff could have their admin done centrally. We would get the report translated before the meeting.

Three moves carry most B2 persuasion, and they are all in the recording: concede (You've got a point, but…), reframe (As I see it…), and challenge with a question (Isn't that a bit…?).

Keep advice and advise apart. Advice is the uncountable noun; advise is the verb, and it is followed by a person, or by to + infinitive: I would advise you to wait.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences, most from the two recordings.

Well, you've got a point, but …
The commonest concession in spoken English.

Yes, but on the other hand …
Balancing your own earlier point.

As I see it, if a teacher is motivating, students won't waste time.
Marking an opinion as yours.

It seems to me that teachers have to work pretty hard.
A softer version of the same move.

Personally, I think a good teacher is quite strict.
Claiming the opinion clearly.

Isn't that kind of teacher a bit old-fashioned?
A challenge shaped as a question.

I'm all for having fun, but I want more than that.
Agreeing in principle, objecting in practice.

It has been argued that perks pay for themselves.
Passive: no arguer named.

Staff could have their admin done centrally.
Causative in a proposal.

I would advise you to wait until the figures are published.
Advise somebody to do something.

steps.title: Changing somebody's mind in four moves
steps.html:
1. The other person has said that a good teacher is strict.
  2. Concede first. If you begin by disagreeing, they stop listening: You've got a point — nobody learns much in a class with no rules.
  3. Reframe. Move the question rather than answering theirs: As I see it, though, the issue is not strictness but motivation.
  4. Challenge with a question. A question is harder to refuse than a statement: Isn't a strict teacher just solving the same problem more slowly?
  5. Offer the arrangement. Say what would actually be done: Their marking could be done centrally, which would give them the time to plan better lessons. Concede, reframe, challenge, propose.

steps.title: Write a summary.
steps.sub: 120–150 words summarising the argument in the first recording: what makes a good teacher. Report both positions and where they ended up. Do not add your own view.
steps.html:
• Open by saying what the speakers were asked to do.
  • Report each position, using reporting verbs: <i>argued, held, conceded, accepted, suggested</i>.
  • Use the passive at least twice: <i>it was pointed out that…</i>
  • State where they ended up.
  • Add nothing of your own — a summary reports.

Useful language

  • The two speakers were asked to agree on …
  • M began by arguing that … , while J took the view that …
  • It was pointed out that …
  • M conceded that … , and J accepted …
  • The list they finally agreed on was …
  • Neither speaker's original list survived intact.
steps.modelHtml:
What makes a good teacher: a summary

Two speakers were asked to agree on the five most important qualities in a teacher, and began some distance apart.

M argued that patience and kindness matter most, on the grounds that learning is not as easy as teachers assume. J accepted the point but held that these are not enough on their own: a teacher also needs good ideas, and the ability to plan something that will actually make a difference.

M then conceded that a fun lesson is not automatically a useful one. J went further, suggesting that a teacher can be too nice and that a good one is quite strict. This was challenged as old-fashioned, and it was argued instead that a motivating teacher removes the problem strictness is meant to solve.

The list they finally agreed on was motivating, supportive, creative, hard-working and well organised. Neither original list survived.
